title: The Five Precepts — The Foundation of a Peaceful Life
lines: Amitabha. Welcome, dear friends, who have come here to quiet the heart and listen to the Dharma.
The Buddha taught lay followers to keep the Five Precepts, the foundation of a peaceful and happy life.
The first precept is not to kill, to cherish the life of every being as we cherish our own.
The second precept is not to steal, not to take what has not been given to us.
The third precept is to avoid sexual misconduct, to stay faithful and honor the happiness of the family.
The fourth precept is not to lie, but to speak words that are true, gentle, and bring people together.
The fifth precept is to avoid intoxicants, so the mind stays clear and awake.
When we keep the Five Precepts, we protect not only ourselves but bring peace to our loved ones and to society.
The precepts are like a fence around the garden of the mind, so the seeds of goodness can grow each day.

title: The Law of Cause and Effect
lines: Dear friends, as we sow, so shall we reap: sow the wind and reap the storm, sow goodness and reap goodness.
Every thought, every word, every action of ours today is a seed for tomorrow.
Those who understand cause and effect do not blame heaven or others, but turn back to improve themselves.
When hardship comes, accept it with a calm mind and plant new seeds of goodness.
When good times come, do not grow proud; be grateful and share your blessings with others.
Never neglect a good deed because it is small, and never do a wrong deed because it is small.
Blessings do not fall from the sky; they are cultivated by our own hands and our own hearts.

title: The Four Immeasurables: Loving-kindness, Compassion, Joy, Equanimity
lines: The Buddha taught us to nurture four boundless states of mind: loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Loving-kindness is love itself, the wish that all people and all beings may be happy.
Compassion is the tender wish to help others move beyond their suffering.
Joy is rejoicing in the happiness of others, without envy when we see them succeed.
Equanimity is letting go, holding no grudges and making no distinction between near and far.
When the heart holds all four, wherever we go, we bring springtime with us.
Begin with a smile, a kind word, a helping hand for the person beside you.

title: Filial Piety — The Gift of Our Parents
lines: Of all good deeds, caring for our parents is the greatest.
Our parents gave us life and raised us, never counting the hardships they endured.
Some search far away for the Buddha, forgetting that the parents at home are two living Buddhas.
Filial piety is not only providing food and clothing, but bringing peace to our parents' hearts.
Living kindly, caring for our health, and speaking gently is the most precious gift we can offer them.
Today, please call your parents and ask after them with a few gentle words.

title: Greed, Anger, Delusion — The Three Poisons of the Mind
lines: The Buddha taught that most human suffering arises from three poisons in the mind: greed, anger, and delusion.
Greed is wanting more and never having enough, so the heart is never at rest.
Anger is rage and impatience; a single spark of anger can burn down a whole forest of merit.
Delusion is not seeing the truth clearly, and so chasing after things that do not last.
The medicine for greed is generosity, contentment, and sharing.
The medicine for anger is compassion, patience, and putting ourselves in another's place.
The medicine for delusion is wisdom: learning diligently, listening deeply, and reflecting.
Each day we let go of a little greed, a little anger, a little delusion, we come a little closer to happiness.

title: Impermanence — Cherishing the Present
lines: Everything in this world is impermanent: what comes together will part, what is born will pass away.
Understanding impermanence, we do not suffer too much in loss, nor cling too tightly in gain.
Impermanence is also a chance, because today's suffering will pass too.
Cherish your loved ones while they are beside you, and say words of love while you still can.
Do not leave for tomorrow the good you can do today.
To live fully in the present moment is to live mindfully.

title: The Four Noble Truths
lines: After his awakening, the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths.
The first is the truth of suffering: life holds suffering, old age, sickness, separation, and unfulfilled longing.
The second is the truth of its cause: suffering arises from craving and clinging.
The third is the truth of its end: suffering can cease, bringing peace and liberation.
The fourth is the truth of the path: the way to end suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path.
Like a skilled physician, the Buddha named the illness, its cause, its cure, and the medicine.

title: The Noble Eightfold Path
lines: The Noble Eightfold Path is eight right ways that help us live in peace in this very life.
Right View is seeing clearly, understanding cause and effect and the nature of impermanence.
Right Intention is thinking with a pure heart, free of greed, hatred, and the wish to harm.
Right Speech is speaking words that are true, gentle, and helpful.
Right Action is acting with goodness, never harming anyone's life or property.
Right Livelihood is earning a living through honest work.
Right Effort is diligently doing good and letting go of what is harmful.
Right Mindfulness is staying awake, knowing clearly what we think, say, and do.
Right Concentration is a mind that is calm and steady, unshaken by outer conditions.

title: The Ten Wholesome Deeds
lines: Followers of the Buddha practice the ten wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind each day.
Of body: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct.
Of speech: no lying, no divisive words, no harsh words, no idle gossip.
Of mind: no greed, no hatred, no deluded or wrong views.
Keeping the ten wholesome deeds, the body is healthy, the family harmonious, and the heart at peace.
Goodness is never far away; it lives in our words and actions every day.

title: Knowing When Enough Is Enough
lines: As the old saying goes: know what is enough and you will always have enough; wait for enough and it will never come.
Happiness is not in having much, but in cherishing what we already have.
A simple meal with family, a peaceful night's sleep, these are already great blessings.
When the heart is content, we have time to love, to help, and to practice.
Today, please take a moment to thank life for its simple gifts.

title: Patience — The Strength of Gentleness
lines: Patience is not weakness; it is the strength of one who is master of oneself.
A single angry word can wound another person for many years.
When anger rises, take a deep breath, smile, and wait for the heart to settle.
Repaying hatred with hatred only piles it higher; repaying hatred with kindness makes it melt away.
Those who are patient have a warm home, loyal friends, and work that flows smoothly.

title: Reciting the Buddha's Name — Keeping the Mind Pure
lines: Reciting the Buddha's name is remembering the Buddha, remembering his compassion and wisdom.
Each recitation of Namo Amitabha Buddha is like a cool drop of water soothing a troubled heart.
Walking, standing, lying down, or sitting, we can always recite the Buddha's name in our hearts.
When the mind is pure, the land is pure; when the heart is at peace, every place is a temple.
Let us join our palms together and gently recite: Namo Amitabha Buddha.

title: Generosity — Planting Seeds of Blessing
lines: Generosity is sharing what we have with those who need it.
There is the gift of wealth, the gift of the Dharma, and the gift of fearlessness, which brings others peace of mind.
A smile or a word of encouragement is also a gift, and everyone can give it.
When we give with a joyful heart, expecting nothing in return, the merit is boundless.
Giving does not make us poorer; it makes our hearts richer.

title: Mindfulness in Daily Life
lines: Mindfulness is knowing clearly what we are doing in the present moment.
When eating, know that you are eating. When walking, know that you are walking.
A single mindful breath is enough to bring us back to ourselves.
Mindfulness helps us hurry less and worry less about what has not yet come.
Try pausing for a moment: breathe in deeply, breathe out slowly, and smile.

title: Loving Speech
lines: Kind words cost nothing, so choose your words to bring joy to one another.
Loving speech is gentle and truthful, and it comes from a caring heart.
A word of praise at the right moment can lift someone's whole day.
Before speaking, ask yourself: is it true, is it helpful, is it kind?
Guarding our speech is also guarding our own merit.

title: Letting Go to Find Peace
lines: Some things hurt more the tighter we hold them; only when we let go do we feel light.
Letting go is not abandoning our responsibilities; it is not clinging to our sorrows.
Let the past be the past, and wish peace to those who have gone.
When the heart opens wide, there is room for new joy to enter.
Today, please set down one small sorrow in your heart.

title: Forgiveness — A Gift to Ourselves
lines: Forgiving others is untying the rope that binds our own heart.
Holding on to hatred is like grabbing a hot coal to throw at someone; our own hand is burned first.
Everyone makes mistakes, and everyone deserves a chance to change.
Forgiveness does not mean forgetting; it means not letting the past torment the present.
May every resentment be dissolved, and may every heart find peace.

title: The Family as a Place of Practice
lines: The family is the first place we learn to love and to forgive.
A shared meal and a caring word are the foundation of happiness.
When husband and wife give way to each other and children listen, that home will surely be at peace.
Practice is never far away; it is in how we treat our loved ones.
May every family always be warm and harmonious.

title: Doing Good Every Day
lines: Do one small good deed each day, and in a year you will have done three hundred sixty-five.
Giving your seat to an elder, helping a child cross the street, all of these are merit.
You need not wait to be rich to do good; all it takes is a caring heart.
Good deeds done quietly bring blessings all the deeper.
Today, please do something kind for someone beside you.

title: Gratitude
lines: Be grateful to our parents, teachers, friends, and even those we have never met.
The rice we eat holds the labor of farmers; the clothes we wear hold the work of craftsmen.
A grateful person always sees life as full of precious things.
Gratitude makes our hearts softer and happier.
Let us join our palms together and give thanks for all that we have.

title: Peace Within
lines: Peace is not the absence of storms, but a steady mind in the midst of them.
Life has its rises and falls, just as the moon waxes and wanes.
When the mind is calm, everything looks beautiful; when the mind is troubled, everywhere feels like suffering.
Take a few minutes each day to sit quietly and listen to your breath.
May all of you always find peace within your own hearts.

title: Closing Prayer
lines: May the merit of this practice extend to all beings everywhere.
May our parents and grandparents be healthy, live long, and be at peace.
May the sick soon recover, and may those who suffer soon find comfort.
May your families always be harmonious, your children devoted, and your work prosperous.
May the world be at peace, and may all beings be happy.
Namo Shakyamuni Buddha, our fundamental teacher.
